title: Load synthesis and adapter onramp - POC kickoff
next_steps: Redwood to share initial harness adapter template and sample payloads (Jordan) - due 2026-10-04
Customer to share 3 canonical scripts + token distribution (Ana) - due 2026-10-02
Schedule live throughput run next week (Priya) - proposed 2026-10-06
action_items: Jordan Lee: upload harness adapter example and README to shared drive; due 2026-10-04
Ana Morales: provide three customer scripts and representative seq length histogram; due 2026-10-02
Priya Nair: prepare baseline config for streaming and non-streaming runs and expected metrics sheet; due 2026-10-05
summary: Kickoff to scope POC for load synthesis and adapter onramp. Customer will provide real scripts; Redwood will provide harness adapter examples and plan streaming vs non-streaming benchmark matrix. Main constraints: PHI concerns, VPC private deployment possibility, want p95 < 150ms for short chat paths and throughput target of 1200 requests/min at 512 token average. Agreement on acceptance criteria and next week's live runs.
topics: Harness adapter requirements and sample formats
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro — Jordan from Redwood, with Priya and Ethan on the call. Ana, Samir, Mei, David — thanks for making time.
[00:10] Ana Morales: Hi, yeah thanks. We're excited to get started, we've been looking at your benchmarks and want to validate on our workload.
[00:22] Priya Nair: Great. The goal today is to nail down acceptance criteria, what scripts you'll hand us, and whether we'll run streaming or non-streaming mode for the first pass.
[00:35] Samir Patel: Quick context — we're ClarityHealth, building an assistant for clinicians to summarize patient notes, there is PHI so we'll likely start with Private (VPC) deployment. Latency is important for short queries.
[00:48] Mei Chen: Security check — we need SOC2 plus audit logs, and customer-managed KMS. Would need to validate with our security team, but want to surface it early.
[01:02] Jordan Lee: That's fine, we have Private deployment options and KMS/HSM integrations. We'll attach SG docs, but Priya can highlight what we usually need for an onramp.
[01:13] Priya Nair: For harness adapter, we accept a few patterns: plain-text scripts, JSON payloads (prompt + metadata), or a small client-runner that emits the sequence and expects a chunked stream. We typically provide a Python adapter template.
[01:28] David Ortiz: Our initial scripts are two types: short clinical queries (avg 120 tokens output/200 tokens input) and longer note summarizations (avg 800 tokens output). We care about p95 for short ones.
[01:44] Ethan Cole: Helpful. Can you share histograms for token lengths? That drives batching and kernel selection.
[01:51] Ana Morales: We'll export histograms from our telemetry; Samir will get them to you. We'll also include distribution of concurrency across users.
[02:01] Samir Patel: Quick question — does Redwood prefer streaming for low latency or non-streaming for throughput? We've read mixed guidance.
[02:10] Priya Nair: Short answer: streaming helps perceived latency for long outputs since you get tokens early, but it complicates harness verification and client expectations. For our engine, streaming has slightly higher CPU overhead at scale but better tail latency for user-facing chat. Non-streaming (batch) is simpler and slightly more cost efficient for high-throughput summarization.
[02:33] Jordan Lee: So for your mix — I'd propose a two-track approach: run short chat scripts in streaming mode to validate p95 latency, and run summarization scripts in non-streaming to validate throughput and cost per 1k tokens.
[02:45] Mei Chen: We also need to confirm data residency — the POC will run in our VPC region (eu-west-1). Are there any kernel/hardware differences across regions that could affect numbers?
[02:56] Priya Nair: There can be minor hardware variance; we'll note the exact instance types. For benchmarks we always include the machine profile. We'll pin model version and quantization.
[03:08] Jordan Lee: Acceptance criteria — what do you need to consider this a success?
[03:13] Ana Morales: Three things: (1) p95 latency for short chat <= 150ms, (2) steady throughput 1200 requests/min for 512 avg token workloads with p99 error <= 1%, (3) qualitative answer quality within our internal eval threshold — we'll provide 50 golden cases.
[03:32] Jordan Lee: Okay that's clear. We'll map those to test cases. For (2) we'll need concurrency shape (burst vs steady) and whether you expect cold starts.
[03:42] Samir Patel: We have a diurnal pattern — bursts in morning rounds; for the POC we want to validate steady and a 3-minute burst of 3x baseline. Cold starts happen when we scale up overnight, but warm cache during day.
[03:55] Priya Nair: We'll run two harness scenarios: steady-state and burst. We'll also do a cold-warm restart to measure tail. Our harness supports KV cache warm-up script to reduce cold-start penalty.
[04:08] David Ortiz: About the harness adapter — our engineers write in Go; do you support a Go adapter or do we need to run Python shim?
[04:15] Ethan Cole: We have a Go sample but the most maintained is Python. If you'd prefer Go, we can provide a minimal shim that delegates to our Python harness or a thin HTTP wrapper.
[04:26] Ana Morales: We'll try native Go if possible. Samir will pick one of our engineers to try the adapter.
[04:33] Samir Patel: On telemetry — what metrics should we record client-side vs Redwood-side?
[04:38] Priya Nair: Capture request start/end, token counts, model version, sequence length, and error code. Redwood will provide server-side traces (latency breakdown, queue time, kernel step). We'll align on field names.
[04:52] Mei Chen: For security, we need to agree on redaction patterns. We'll pre-mask PHI fields in the dev set and send synthetic data for the long-run.
[05:02] Jordan Lee: Good plan. For the initial bench we can run with synthetic de-identified data and then a locked-down private run for a small sample of real notes under an NDA.
[05:13] Ana Morales: Timeline question — how fast can we get a first-run?
[05:18] Jordan Lee: If you share scripts and histograms by Friday (Oct 2), we can have adapter sample and baseline configs by Oct 4, and a first live run the week of Oct 5 — likely Oct 6 as proposed.
[05:30] David Ortiz: That sounds good. Do you require additional infra or service accounts?
[05:35] Priya Nair: For VPC private POC we'll need connectivity info (peering or bastion) and a service account with limited access. We'll share a checklist.
[05:44] Samir Patel: How does KV cache warm-up work? Does the harness pre-populate caches?
[05:50] Ethan Cole: Yes, the harness can replay prefixes to populate KV cache. We'll coordinate the warmup input set; generally a few thousand tokens of representative prefixes are enough. We'll measure cold vs warmed p95.
[06:02] Ana Morales: About pricing for Dedicated — if the POC shows we need reserved capacity, how does the procurement work?
[06:10] Jordan Lee: We'll share pricing lanes: hosted pay-as-you-go, Dedicated reserved capacity with monthly commit, and Private licensing for on-prem. For POC we usually run on hosted or a temporary Dedicated pool depending on region — we'll clarify in the pricing doc.
[06:24] Mei Chen: Any compliance docs we can look at now?
[06:27] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll attach SOC2, our security whitepaper, and the onboarding checklist; I'll drop links in the follow-up.
[06:34] Samir Patel: One technical nit — when streaming, do you support interleaving function calls or tool calls in the stream? We sometimes do structured JSON outputs.
[06:44] Priya Nair: Streaming supports chunked tokens and also structured tool-calls; the harness can validate expected JSON schema, but test harness verification is easier in non-streaming. We'll draft a schema sample.
[06:57] David Ortiz: For the acceptance eval you'll need our golden set; what format do you want?
[07:02] Ethan Cole: CSV with id, input, expected_output and a rubric for fuzz matching is ideal. We'll run automated comparisons and flag regressions.
[07:12] Ana Morales: We'll also include a human-eval pass for 10 samples.
[07:16] Jordan Lee: Great. Now let's outline the benchmark matrix — Priya, can you walk through the columns?
[07:20] Priya Nair: Sure — columns: test_name, mode (streaming/non-streaming), model_version, seq_in_avg, seq_out_avg, concurrency, target_rps, duration, metrics_to_capture (p50,p95,p99,throughput,cost_per_1k), success_threshold. Example: short-chat-streaming, streaming, redwood-v3, 200/120, concurrency 50, target 20rps, duration 10m, p95 <=150ms.
[07:56] Samir Patel: For throughput test, target 1200 requests/min at 512 avg tokens equals 20 rps — sounds right.
[08:03] Priya Nair: We'll also include an error budget test (p99 errors <1%) and a cold-start test where we restart a subset of nodes and measure tails.
[08:12] Ana Morales: How do we measure cost-per-answer?
[08:16] Jordan Lee: We'll capture token counts + hardware cost for the run. For Dedicated we'll estimate amortized GPU-hour cost; for hosted we'll use per-token billing. We'll share a cost calculator.
[08:28] Mei Chen: If we run in our VPC, can you provide telemetry export (S3 logs) for ingestion into our monitoring?
[08:35] Priya Nair: Yes we can push logs to an S3 bucket in your account or stream to a collector. We'll include example config.
[08:44] David Ortiz: Any common pitfalls from previous POCs?
[08:47] Ethan Cole: Two big ones: (1) scripts with embedded randomness causing inconsistent latency and QA outcomes — we ask for fixed seeds; (2) not accounting for caching effects when comparing streaming vs non-streaming.
[09:00] Ana Morales: We'll attach deterministic seeds. Good catch.
[09:04] Jordan Lee: On the harness side, we'll provide a replay tool and a live-driver. The driver can run streaming clients concurrently or batch-run. We'll also provide a validation harness to assert output shapes.
[09:18] Samir Patel: For the adapter, do we need to do auth token rotation? Our infra requires short-lived tokens.
[09:24] Priya Nair: The adapter can handle token rotation; we provide examples for rotating credentials and refreshing. For Private deployments we often wire to an internal vault; we'll include a pattern.
[09:36] Ana Morales: About timeline again — if we do the first run Oct 6, when can we expect a results deck?
[09:41] Jordan Lee: Expect a preliminary results deck within 48 hours of the run, with full annotated traces a few days later.
[09:48] Mei Chen: We'll lock down NDA for the real-data run.
[09:51] Jordan Lee: Understood. We'll circulate paperwork.
[09:55] David Ortiz: One more question — how do we simulate clinical workflow concurrency? It's not uniform, it's per clinician sessions.
[10:02] Priya Nair: The harness supports session-affinity simulation; you can mark sequences as session-bound and maintain KV cache per session. That helps mimic clinician usage and cache hit rates.
[10:13] Samir Patel: That matters a lot. Our cache hit rate will change cost significantly.
[10:18] Ethan Cole: We'll include a session-based run.
[10:22] Ana Morales: Anything else risk-wise? Not that I can think of.
[10:26] Jordan Lee: Let's quickly recap next steps.
[10:29] Jordan Lee: Action items: Jordan to upload adapter template; Ana to send scripts + histograms; Priya to prepare baseline configs; schedule live run Oct 6.
[10:40] Ana Morales: Confirmed. We'll also share a security contact.
[10:43] Mei Chen: I'll be that contact for security review.
[10:46] Jordan Lee: Great — we'll follow up with a calendar invite for Oct 6 and include a checklist & links to docs (SOC2, onboarding checklist, adapter repo).
[10:56] Samir Patel: Thanks everyone, excited to get moving.
[10:59] Jordan Lee: Thanks all, talk soon.
[11:03] [end of recording]
